analysis.one_liner: Requires airlines to refund cancelled or badly changed flights within 48 hours, with penalties.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with no cosponsors in the final two weeks of the Congress, never got a committee hearing or a floor vote and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it a legal violation for an airline or ticket seller to keep your money when it cancels a flight or changes it by three or more hours domestically (six internationally), changes the airport, adds a stop, or significantly downgrades the aircraft. Refunds would have to go back to the original payment method within 48 hours for card payments or 14 days for cash, and airlines that failed could face a civil penalty equal to ten times the ticket price. If a passenger voluntarily accepted a rebooking or voucher instead, no refund would be owed.
analysis.who_benefits: Passengers whose flights are cancelled or drastically changed. Today, getting money back depends on airline discretion and slow federal enforcement; the bill would have made a full cash refund a legal right with a hard deadline, enforceable through penalties.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it an unfair or deceptive practice for an airline, foreign carrier, or ticket agent to fail to refund a ticket when the flight is cancelled or significantly changed [S2, S3].
Requires the refund in the original payment form within 48 hours for card payments or 14 days for cash or check payments [S3].
Defines 'significantly changed' to cover a shift of 3 hours or more for domestic flights (6 hours international), a different airport, added stops, or a significantly downgraded aircraft [S3].
Sets a civil penalty for a missed refund at ten times the ticket price, giving the government a strong enforcement tool [S3].
Lets passengers keep a rebooking or other compensation instead of a refund if they voluntarily accept it [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Airlines and ticket agents, which would have to return ticket money quickly after cancellations and big schedule changes instead of offering vouchers first, and would face penalties ten times the ticket price for failing to comply.

drawbacks.text: A strict 48-hour refund deadline could be difficult for airlines to process at scale during mass-cancellation events like storms, potentially slowing the rebooking help passengers need most in the moment [S3].
A penalty of ten times the ticket price on every missed refund could be disproportionate for an individual glitch, though it was designed to make enforcement worthwhile for regulators [S3].

The bill excluded passengers who voluntarily accepted alternative transportation or compensation, so an airline could still steer a stranded traveler into accepting a voucher rather than cash [S2, S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and significant: a guaranteed, fast, cash refund when an airline fails to fly you as promised, backed by meaningful penalties. The compliance burden on airlines is modest compared with what ticket refunds have historically cost them, and the strongest design objections are about penalty calibration and the voucher loophole, not the refund right itself.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its Aviation Subcommittee and sat there; the Congress ended two weeks later without any hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Katie Porter introduced the bill on December 20, 2022, just days after the Southwest Airlines meltdown that canceled thousands of flights over the holidays, and it was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee [S1, S5].
It was referred to the Subcommittee on Aviation the next day, December 21, 2022, and received no further action [S5].
No other member cosponsored the bill [S4].
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the bill died without a hearing, markup, or vote in committee or on the floor [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Airlines and ticket agents came out ahead: they kept the status quo, in which refunds after cancellations depend on airline policy and case-by-case federal enforcement rather than a statutory deadline with penalties, and they face no civil penalty for slow refunds.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Airlines, which keep refund policies discretionary

for.name: Rep. Katie Porter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup on the bill before the Congress ended.

against.name: Aviation Subcommittee of the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no action in the two weeks remaining in the session.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred and no other member of either party cosponsored the bill, so the record shows only a single Democratic sponsor and no measurable party alignment [S4].

industries.note: Airlines would have lost the ability to sit on ticket money after cancellations and would have faced penalties ten times the ticket price for missed refunds. Their interest in keeping refunds discretionary runs directly against passengers' interest in getting cash back quickly.

industries.industry: Ticket agents and online travel sellers
industries.note: The bill applied the refund obligation to ticket agents as well as airlines, so intermediaries that sell tickets would also have been required to turn refunds around within 48 hours on card payments.
